summary: MARPS (Mars Augmented Route Planning System) is turn-by-turn navigation for astronauts on Mars. Inside the helmet, a heads-up display draws the safest route on the ground and shows oxygen, radiation, radio coverage and what to do at each science stop. It reroutes when the astronaut leaves the path or a dust storm hits. Behind the display is a route-planning engine that doesn’t depend on any device, built on real HiRISE terrain data. We show it here in VR, but it could run on any suit display, rover or mission-control screen.
details:
What it does and how it works

MARPS (Mars Augmented Route Planning System) is turn-by-turn navigation for an astronaut exploring Mars on foot. We built it for a 2 × 2 km site mapped by NASA’s HiRISE camera, with glacier margins, “brain terrain” over buried ice, a light-toned ridge and a round pit.

The system has two parts:

  • The route-planning engine. It reads the terrain’s height map and rates every point by slope and surface: over 22° is no-go, 15–22° is caution, and rough ground is avoided. It plans the safest walking route between stops, estimates walking time including climbs, and checks radio line of sight to the hab and relay masts.
    • The route is drawn as a line on the ground ahead of you.
    • A curved HUD inside the visor shows a compass, a minimap, oxygen, radiation dose, radio signal and the next stop.
    • A display on the forearm holds each stop’s science checklist, map layers (slope, ice and others) and mission data.
    • If you walk off the path, the route is recalculated from where you are. Some steps only count on the right ground; for example, drilling only works on mapped ice.
    • When something goes wrong (a dust storm, a solar storm, a suit leak or low oxygen), the system warns you and replans the route home.

Benefits

  • Safer walks: routes avoid dangerous slopes, and the astronaut always knows how far and how long it is back to the hab, compared with the oxygen left.
  • Less to think about: the most important information sits in the centre of view, secondary information further out, and checklists stay on the arm instead of the visor.
  • More science per walk: stops are planned around targets that matter, like buried ice and water-altered minerals. The checklist explains why each step matters, and the instrument readings use real absorption bands for water ice, gypsum and olivine.
  • Staying in contact: the astronaut is warned before walking into a radio dead zone.

Intended impact

Astronauts on Mars will spend hours outside the hab with a 20-minute communication delay to Earth, so they can’t count on mission control to guide them step by step. MARPS shows how real orbital data can become simple, safe guidance in the astronaut’s own view. The engine doesn’t depend on any device, so the same routes and hazard maps could drive a suit display, a rover screen or a mission-control map.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Engine: C# with no device dependencies.
    • HiRISE terrain model DTEEC_079228_2240_079716_2240_A01 and image ESP_079228_2240 (NASA/JPL/University of Arizona);
    • HRSC + MOLA blended elevation for the horizon;
    • radiation dose from Curiosity’s RAD instrument;
    • spectral band positions from lab mineral spectra.
  • Workflow: Unity Version Control and GitHub.
  • Claude Code (AI) helped with the engine’s development, the Unity simulation, and with finding and processing the scientific data. Terrain and imagery are from NASA’s HiRISE (NASA/JPL/University of Arizona) and HRSC/MOLA. The 3D astronaut and habitat models are from Sketchfab (CC BY 4.0) and the astronaut hand from TurboSquid (royalty-free license); full credits are in the app. The logo, the Mars sky and the ice map were made by our team.

How it’s creative

Instead of a map you have to stop and read, the route is drawn on the ground ahead of you, like a car navigation app reimagined for walking on Mars. The orbital ice map does more than decorate the scene: it decides where tasks can be done, and the radio coverage changes as you move. The whole thing is a working prototype you can walk through, not just a concept.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: slope limits, oxygen use (which goes up with speed and climbing), the radiation dose, and always knowing the way home.
  • Readability: text has to stay legible over bright Martian sand and in a dust storm.
  • Realism and honesty: real terrain and real data where they exist. Anything simulated, such as the minerals at each stop, the storms and the suit faults, is labelled as simulated in the app’s credits.
  • Performance: everything runs on a standalone Quest 2.
  • Science value: stops chosen around ice and evidence of past water.
